nameStory: Cushion spurge gets its name from its distinctive growth habit - it forms neat, rounded cushions or mounds that look like living pillows in the garden. The 'spurge' part comes from the old word 'spurgen,' meaning to purge or cleanse, referring to the medicinal uses of plants in this family (though don't try this at home - they can be quite toxic!).
description: Cushion spurge is a compact, dome-shaped perennial that looks like someone carefully sculpted a bright green mound in your garden. This well-behaved plant grows to about 18 inches tall and wide, forming dense clumps of oval leaves on upright stems. In spring and early summer, it puts on a spectacular show with masses of tiny chartreuse-yellow flowers that seem to glow against the green foliage. It's a popular garden plant that occasionally escapes cultivation in New England.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms perfect dome-shaped cushions or mounds, like a natural hedge trimmed into a ball. The plant is densely branched and compact, never sprawling or getting leggy.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Clusters of tiny acid-yellow to chartreuse flowers that lack true petals but are surrounded by bright yellow-green bracts. The flower heads sit at the tips of stems and create a stunning golden cap over the green foliage.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to oblong leaves about 1-2 inches long, arranged alternately up the stem. They feel smooth and slightly thick, with a fresh green color that provides perfect contrast to the bright flowers.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Break a stem and you'll see the telltale spurge trait - milky white sap that oozes out. This latex can irritate skin, so observe but don't touch with bare hands.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small three-lobed capsules that split open when ripe, explosively shooting seeds several feet away with an audible 'pop' if you're listening carefully.

habitat: In New England, cushion spurge is primarily found as an escaped garden plant in disturbed areas, along roadsides, and in abandoned home sites. It prefers well-drained soils and full to partial sun, often appearing near old foundations or in areas where gardens once flourished. You might spot it in waste places and edge habitats where it has naturalized from nearby cultivation.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges bright green, and the spectacular flower show begins in late spring with masses of glowing yellow-green blooms that can last for weeks.
seasonality.summer: Flowers may continue into early summer, followed by the development of seed capsules. The neat mounded form is most obvious during this season.
seasonality.fall: Foliage may take on reddish or bronze tints before the plant goes dormant. Seeds are dispersed as capsules split open.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, leaving no visible trace above ground until spring emergence.

funFact: Cushion spurge has explosive seed pods that can launch seeds up to 15 feet away with enough force to make an audible popping sound - it's like the plant has its own tiny seed cannons ensuring the next generation spreads far from the parent!
confusionNotes: The dome-shaped growth habit and bright chartreuse spring flowers make cushion spurge fairly distinctive, but other spurges might confuse beginners. Remember: if it looks like a perfectly trimmed green basketball covered in glowing yellow flowers, you've found cushion spurge. The neat, compact mounding habit sets it apart from the sprawling or upright forms of other spurges.
contextualKnowledge: Like all spurges, this plant produces a milky latex sap that can cause skin irritation and is toxic if ingested. Despite being in the same family as poinsettias, the relationship isn't obvious until you notice the similar flower structure - what look like petals are actually colorful bracts surrounding tiny flowers.
compareHints: Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form. While cypress spurge forms colonies of thin, needle-like leaves, cushion spurge has broader oval leaves and stays in discrete clumps. The bright chartreuse flower color and cushion growth habit make it unique among New England's spurges - most others are either much smaller ground-huggers or tall, lanky plants.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
